articles.title: Ali Asgari Doesn’t Believe in a Bright Future After Iran’s January Massacre – Just ‘A Bit of Light’
articles.summary: Iranian director Ali Asgari has no desire to repeat clichés about great expectations for things to come. “In Iran, we don’t have high hopes for the future anymore,” he states. “We’ve been waiting for good news for so many years, and it never came. But I do believe in these small specks of light. For
body: “Right now, especially in my country, we are forgetting about them. We’re forgetting about our families and helping others. We are surrounded by disaster every day, all the time, always expecting something horrible to happen,” he says.

“When we wake up, we don’t know if we’ll be able to handle it until nighttime. We’re all living in a dangerous world right now. If after watching this film someone goes to their mother and takes her hand, that’s enough.”

Family is certainly on the mind of his protagonist, a kind doctor (played by Misagh Zareh) who becomes disillusioned after his arrest. With his medical practice shut down, he’s ready to end his life. He’s a practical man, though, so he decides to tell his family and make suitable arrangements.
“Some doctors in Iran were the only witnesses to what was really happening after the massacre in January. They faced so much death and saw so many injured. We couldn’t even talk about it,” he notes.
points: Iranian director Ali Asgari has no desire to repeat clichés about great expectations for things to come.
“In Iran, we don’t have high hopes for the future anymore,” he states.
“We’ve been waiting for good news for so many years, and it never came.

articles.title: ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’ Star Adia On Film Debut Opposite Mahershala Ali, Getting Certified as a Doula: ‘Birth Work Fills My Soul’
articles.summary: Twenty-five-year-old newcomer Adia never really imagined becoming a movie star. Growing up, she was focused on becoming a professional dancer before a hip injury derailed that dream. That’s when the high school senior discovered acting.
body: “Things started to fall in place as soon as I started pursuing acting, and it’s just snowballed,” she said. “It’s just very surreal.”
Even so, Adia didn’t picture a career making movies — which makes her big screen debut in the action-drama from filmmaker Bassam Tariq (“Mogul Mowgli”) all the more unexpected.

“ Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,” which debuted on Saturday night at the Toronto International Film Festival, stars two-time Oscar winner Mahershala Ali as Latif, a hired assassin whose secret occupation clashes with his home life when his wife dies suddenly. The film follows Latif as he navigates single fatherhood, including a desperate search for breast milk for his infant daughter. Adia plays Latif’s strong-willed teenage daughter Fatiha, who is forced to grow up quickly as she helps her father care for her younger brother and sister.

“She was just really complex,” Adia said, explaining what drew her to the role. “That’s how young, teenage girls are. But when we see them being portrayed on screen, generally speaking, they are not [complex]. They’re pretty black and white. ‘Oh, she’s just moody, hormonal and thinking about boys, and that’s it.”

articles.title: Jeremy Thomas Remembered as a Filmmaker ‘Full of Stories’ and a ‘Rebel With Taste’: ‘The Canon of His Work Is Unmatched’
articles.summary: Tributes have begun flowing from across the film world for Jeremy Thomas, the legendary British producer who passed away on Friday at the age of 77. Terry Gilliam, who worked with Thomas on “Tideland” and “The Man Who Killed Don Quixote,” told Variety, “Jeremy Thomas loved making movies.
body: Luca Guadagnino, who recently put Thomas on camera for his Venice-bowing documentary “Joie De Vivre” to talk about Italian director Bernardo Bertolucci (with whom he made five films), offered Variety a heartfelt statement about the producer.

Takashi Miike, the Japanese filmmaker who collaborated with Thomas across numerous features, including “Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo,” premiering in Toronto on Monday, sent Variety a message to his dear friend.

“We promised to celebrate the world premiere here in Toronto and have a good drink together,” he said. “This sudden news came out of nowhere, leaving me completely in shock and deeply saddened. Jeremy gave me my wings — he was a great mentor and an irreplaceable friend. Rest in peace for now. Until we meet again.”

articles.title: Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom review – Aardman’s spooky-season caper sparkles with fun
articles.summary: There’s trouble afoot when Shaun’s pumpkin-supersizing serum ends up in a balding farmer’s hair growth bottle in this third cinematic adventure. Summer is over and Halloween is on the way … not for a fair bit, of course, but if all the UK’s Halloween merch and continuing pop culture content is up…
body: The pitchfork-wielding villagers of Mossy Bottom are hilariously stunned at the terrifying appearance of a rampaging, hairy beast who has been spotted in the outlying fields and woodlands at the very moment that the farmer himself has mysteriously disappeared. Has the beast somehow kidnapped or eaten the farmer? It is a nightmarish mystery that will need every ounce of Shaun and his pals’ courage and ingenuity to sort out, not to mention that of the vet, who uses a hi-tech DNA machine to examine the genetic provenance of a piece of the beast’s fur she has managed to snip off.

It is a love story of sorts, perhaps a little like that of Beauty and the Beast, but about two people who for most the story’s running time don’t know that they are going to be in love. As for the sheep, their faces convey amazingly distinct expressions and moods with just a few deft movements. It’s sharp, smart, funny and precise; there is nothing woolly about it.

articles.title: Kaelen Ohm Talks Bringing Inner Extreme Skier to Film Roles: “I Want to Find the Steeper Hill to Go Down”
articles.summary: Star turns in 'Hit & Run,' 'From' and 'The Betrayers' thriller this year at the Toronto Film Festival have got Ohm onto everyone's call sheets in Canada.
body: Kaelen Ohm says what got her as a fearless young skier better and faster down mountains in small-town Canada now drives her climb onto everyone’s call sheets as a go-for-it actor, filmmaker and musician.

That need to go her own way as an actor and artist over two decades includes early TV roles in Hell on Wheels, Taken and Murdoch Mysteries. “Often you are playing against a show’s leads, so I got to walk in and watch Brendan Fraser work for a day,” Ohm recalls of a one-episode stint on Condor alongside the Oscar-winning The Whale star.

Ohm’s breakout TV role came in 2020 as Danielle, a gifted American dancer killed in a car accident in the first episode of Netflix’s bingeable mystery Hit & Run. Her husband, played by Fauda star Lior Raz, then investigates her unexplained death as Ohm’s character appears in flashbacks.

“That was an act of God,” she says of first auditioning for Raz and The Killing and The Handmaid’s Tale creators in New York City. “I thought I’m going to meet these incredible creatives with decades-long careers and I was the least nervous I’d ever been because I thought there’s no way this will work out for me.”
points: Star turns in 'Hit & Run,' 'From' and 'The Betrayers' thriller this year at the Toronto Film Festival have got Ohm onto everyone's call sheets in Canada.

articles.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother review – Mahershala Ali is a grieving hitman in soulful thriller
articles.summary: Toronto film festival: the two-time Oscar-winner is an unusual killer in a compelling mix of pulpy action and family drama. Latif, the solemn hitman played soulfully by Mahershala Ali, carries diapers in his kill kit.
body: Those contradictions are on full striking display in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’s opening moments, an explosive close-quarters brawl in a restroom, after which Latif uses the baby wipes to clean up the mess he made with that blade. It’s a lovely image, in a film filled with so many, cutting right through the tension within this character. It also feels like a wink to the audience from Ali and writer/director Bassam Tariq, a way for them to acknowledge right off the top the distracting mess made by that other Blade.

Tariq and Ali were collaborating on Marvel’s Blade reboot. Ali was announced to star as the vampire-slayer formerly played by Wesley Snipes all the way back in 2019. Tariq signed on to write and direct in 2021 but departed a year later. Ali recently revealed that, after being strung along for seven years in development, the reboot was not happening. It’s easy to assume that some of the ideas Tariq and Ali had for Blade made their way into this new collaboration, in which Ali gets to finally wield a blade and John Cho, of Harold and Kumar fame, stuns as a vampiric foe. The echoes and parallels are there but minimal, perhaps even coincidental.

articles.title: ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’ Review: Mahershala Ali Is a Marvel in a Gripping Crime Film With a Big, Aching Heart
articles.summary: The two-time Oscar winner plays a devout Muslim and contract killer forced to care for his three kids after his wife dies in Bassam Tariq's Texas-set thriller.
body: Latif is a strong, quiet man and lethal with a knife, but he’s also a father. When his wife Khadijah (Shakirah DeMesier) suddenly dies, leaving him as the sole parent of his three children, his work and family life collide. Soon he has to answer to Fatiha (Adia), his thoughtful and intelligent adolescent daughter, who challenges him with questions he doesn’t want to answer. His devout son Qadir (Jahleel Kamara) — still full of the energy and optimism of childhood — forces Latif to confront his lapsed faith. Then there’s Aziza, a nursing baby robbed of both the nourishment and comfort of her mother.

Latif must change his priorities rapidly. Suddenly, life for him becomes a constant search for breast milk to feed his daughter. Fatiha tries to give her sister formula, but the baby can’t digest it. Her constant hunger is a living manifestation of Latif’s inability to take his wife’s place. More comfortable in the role of provider, Latif has to learn how to tap into his nurturing side. Writer and director Bassam Tariq gives us a figure rarely seen on American screens: a Black Muslim man portrayed tenderly, with his family and faith as an anchor.

articles.title: ‘How We Stand’ Director on Recasting 1950s American Indians Relocation Legacy: “It’s Such an Epic Story”
articles.summary: Marie Clements' drama about a single mother and three daughters separated by tragedy after resettling for new lives in 1950s Los Angeles will world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival.
body: Los Angeles is home to a sizable urban indigenous community after the U.S. federal government in the 1950s launched its Native American Relocation Program that led American Indians to leave rural reservations for what they hoped would be better jobs and lives in major cities.

“It’s such an epic story, as universally we all want to go somewhere just to have a new beginning, to create a better future for our children and our families,” Clements tells The Hollywood Reporter ahead of her film’s Sept. 13 world premiere at TIFF. That simple dream became a nightmare of extreme poverty and trauma in How We Stand, which also stars in the role of the three sisters: Amber Midthunder as Jessie, Alyssa Wapanatâhk as Miranda and Isabel DeRoy-Olson as Janey.

Having taken shelter in a native American community in “the tombs,” or the cemented riverways of Los Angeles, violent tragedy strikes Angela, which leads to her daughters becoming separated and sent down divergent paths in life before they are reunited in 1970s LA during a dramatic flood scene.
